q: How many usable host addresses are in a /27 IPv4 subnet?
why: A /27 has 32 addresses. The first is the network address and the last is the broadcast, so 30 can be given to hosts.

q: Why is 'snmp-server community public RW' a serious finding?
options: Anyone who guesses the default string can read and change the device
why: Default community strings are the first thing tried. A read-write string lets someone change configuration.

q: A host sends SYNs to 40 different ports and gets resets or silence. What is the most careful reading?
options: A scan-like pattern: check whether the host is yours and what else it touched
why: That shape fits a scan, but monitoring tools and misconfigured clients look similar. It is a lead to verify.

q: Ping to 8.8.8.8 works but 'example.com' fails to load. Where do you look first?
why: If an IP works and the name doesn't, the path is fine and name resolution is the fault.

q: A single TCP stream with a 64 KB window on an 80 ms link is limited to roughly what?
options: About 6.5 Mbps (window divided by round-trip time)
why: Throughput can't exceed window divided by round-trip time: 64 KB x 8 / 0.08 s is about 6.5 Mbps, however fast the link is.

q: You can't reach a file server. Which order of checks is best?
options: Reinstall the OS, then check cables
Link and address first, then gateway, then name, then port, then the application
Change several settings at once to save time
why: Working up the layers finds the lowest broken layer quickly, and one change at a time lets you know what fixed it.

q: A router-on-a-stick has subinterfaces g0/0.10 and g0/0.20. What does 'encapsulation dot1Q 10' do?
options: Tells the subinterface to handle frames tagged with VLAN 10
Turns the port into an access port
why: dot1Q followed by an id tells that subinterface which VLAN tag it serves. Add 'native' only for the untagged VLAN. The subinterface address then becomes that VLAN's gateway.

q: Switch A trunks with native VLAN 99 and switch B with native VLAN 1. What happens?
options: Untagged frames land in different VLANs on each side and the switches log a mismatch
The trunk will not come up at all, ever
why: The trunk can still pass tagged traffic, but untagged frames are put into different VLANs, which leaks traffic between them and breaks things quietly. Make both ends match.

q: A /24 route from RIP (AD 120) and a /16 route from OSPF (AD 110) both contain the destination. Which wins?
options: RIP, because the /24 is more specific
why: Longest prefix match comes first; administrative distance only chooses between routes for the same prefix.

q: Which cable gives 10 Gbps over a full 100 m run?
why: Cat 6 manages 10 Gbps only on short runs (about 37 to 55 m). Cat 6a is specified for 100 m at 10 Gbps. Cat 7 is not a TIA category.

q: In DHCP DORA, which two messages are always broadcast by the client?
why: The client has no address yet, so Discover and Request go to 255.255.255.255. The server's Offer and Acknowledge are usually unicast to the client unless the client asked for broadcast replies.

q: What are the four steps of DHCP, in order?
why: The client broadcasts Discover, a server replies with an Offer, the client asks for it with a Request, and the server confirms with an Acknowledge.

q: A client gets an address but cannot reach the internet. Which DHCP setting is the most likely to be missing?
why: Without the router option a client can talk to its own subnet only.

q: Why is a second DHCP server on the same network a problem?
options: Clients may take addresses and settings from either one, so some get wrong ones
DHCP cannot run twice on one switch
why: Whichever server answers first wins, so clients end up with mixed or conflicting settings.

q: Which design step comes before choosing devices?
options: Designing the logical network: addresses, VLANs and zones
why: The logical design tells you what you need. Buying first locks you into hardware that may not fit.

q: You have 40 hosts today and expect 25% growth. How many hosts should the subnet be sized for?
why: 40 x 1.25 = 50. Then add two for the network and broadcast addresses, which gives a /26 (62 usable).

q: Where should guest Wi-Fi sit?
options: On its own VLAN with internet access only
why: Guests must not reach internal subnets. Isolate them and allow only the internet.

q: Why must different sites use non-overlapping address blocks?
options: So they can be routed or joined later
why: Overlapping blocks cannot be routed to each other without NAT workarounds, and a merger or VPN makes that painful.

q: What does ARP do?
options: Maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local network
why: Hosts broadcast 'who has this IP?' and the owner replies with its MAC. Troubleshooting is ICMP (ping). The source glossary gets this wrong.

q: Which IEEE standard covers a WMAN (WiMAX)?
why: 802.11 is Wi-Fi (WLAN), 802.15 is Bluetooth and Zigbee (WPAN), 802.16 is WiMAX (WMAN), 802.3 is Ethernet.

q: What is the modern default port for SMB file sharing?
why: Ports 137 to 139 are legacy NetBIOS. Modern SMB uses TCP 445. 3389 is RDP.

q: Which remote-access protocol sends passwords in clear text?
why: Telnet (port 23) has no encryption. Use SSH (port 22).

q: A device forwards frames out one port using a MAC address table. What is it?
why: A hub repeats to every port, a switch learns MAC addresses, a router uses IP addresses.

q: What is a WISP?
why: An ISP that delivers service by radio, often fixed wireless. The source glossary confused it with a cellular WWAN.

q: Which transport suits live voice or a game better, and why?
options: UDP, because late packets are useless and overhead is low
why: A retransmitted packet from two seconds ago is no use in a live call. UDP skips retransmission and has lower overhead.

q: A switch builds its MAC table from...
options: The destination address of each frame
The source address of each frame
why: It records which port each source address was seen on, then uses the destination address to look up where to send.

q: Which switch becomes the spanning tree root?
options: The one with the most ports
The lowest bridge ID (priority, then MAC)
why: The election is by bridge ID only. Priority is compared first, then the MAC address.

q: Two BGP routes: A has local preference 100 and a 2-AS path, B has local preference 200 and a 3-AS path. Which wins?
why: Local preference is checked before AS-path length, so B wins.

q: A capture shows SYN packets and no SYN-ACK replies. The safest conclusion is...
options: The attempts got no answer; check the firewall, the host, the route and where the capture was taken
why: No reply has several possible causes, and a capture on one side may not see the reply at all.
